unit.title: Support, resistance and chart patterns
unit.description: Price zones, trendlines, chart patterns and false breakouts

steps.title: What they are
steps.body:
• **Support:** a zone where falls have stalled several times because buyers show up.
• **Resistance:** a zone where rises have stalled because sellers show up.

They are the market’s memory: someone who bought at €50 and watched it drop to €40 will want to «get out without a loss» if it gets back to €50. Round numbers and all-time highs also attract orders.

steps.title: How to draw them
steps.body:
1. Daily or weekly charts work best.
2. Look for zones where the price has turned at least **2–3 times**.
3. Draw a **zone** (a narrow rectangle), not a line to the cent.
4. More touches and more volume = more relevant.
5. Old, distant levels carry less weight.

steps.title: What they’re for
steps.body: They tell you where buying or selling may appear and, above all, where your idea stops being valid: the stop goes on the other side of the support and the target just before the resistance.
steps.key: Support is where buyers showed up before; resistance is where sellers did.
steps.tip: Draw them as zones, not as razor-sharp lines.

steps.title: Switching roles
steps.body:
When the price clearly breaks through resistance, that zone often turns into **support**. And the other way round: broken support often becomes **resistance**.

Whoever sold at resistance and watched the price rise will want to buy back if it returns; whoever bought at the broken support will want to get out «without a loss».

steps.title: The return to the level
steps.body:
After a breakout, the price often comes back to **test** the level before moving on. Bulkowski calls it a *throwback* if the breakout was upwards and a *pullback* if it was downwards.

In the head and shoulders, for example, the price returns to the neckline **68 %** of the time.

steps.title: How it’s used
steps.body: If broken resistance holds as support on the return, the breakout gains credibility. If the price clearly moves back inside, the breakout was false and the idea has failed.
steps.key: Broken support often becomes resistance, and broken resistance becomes support.
steps.tip: What used to be the ceiling can be the new floor.

steps.title: How to draw one
steps.body:
• **Uptrend:** connects at least **two higher lows**; a third touch confirms it.
• **Downtrend:** connects at least two **lower highs**.
• Don’t force it: if it has to cut through several candles to fit, it’s not a good line.

steps.title: Channels and slope
steps.body:
A parallel line through the highs of an uptrend forms a **channel**: the lower edge acts as support and the upper edge as resistance.

Very steep lines break quickly; those at around 30–45 degrees tend to hold longer. On charts covering several years, use a logarithmic scale.

steps.title: Breaking the line
steps.body: Breaking a trendline is **not** a trend change on its own: a sideways phase may begin. Combine it with the structure of highs and lows.
steps.key: An uptrend line connects higher lows; as long as it holds, the trend continues.
steps.tip: If you have to force the line to touch the points, the line is in your head.

steps.title: The pattern
steps.body:
After a **rise**, three peaks: the middle one (the **head**) higher than the two on the sides (the **shoulders**), which are of similar height.

The **neckline** connects the lows between the peaks. The pattern **is confirmed** when the price **closes below** the neckline. The **inverse H&S** is the bullish version, after a fall.

steps.title: The target
steps.body:
Classic target: the distance from the head to the neckline, projected downwards from the breakout.

Example: head at €120, neckline at €100. Height €20 → target €80. Bulkowski suggests a more cautious one, using half the height → €90.

steps.title: What the data say (Bulkowski)
steps.body:
• Average fall after the breakout: **16 %**.
• Fails (doesn’t even fall 5 %): **19 %**.
• Returns to the neckline: **68 %**.
• Reaches the classic target: only **51 %**.
steps.tip: An H&S without a breakout is just a nicely shaped mountain.

steps.title: M and W
steps.body:
• **Double top (M):** two peaks at a similar height, separated by a trough. It’s confirmed when the price **breaks the low of the trough**.
• **Double bottom (W):** two similar lows. It’s confirmed when the price **clears the high in between**.

Classic target: the height of the pattern, projected from the breakout.

steps.title: The big mistake
steps.body:
Calling any pair of peaks a «double top» **before** the breakout. Many double tops «in the making» turn out to be simple pauses before new highs.

Without a break of the trough, all you have is two peaks.

steps.title: An example
steps.body: Double bottom with lows at €40 and a high in between at €50. Height: €10. On a close above €50, the classic target is €60. If it then closes clearly below €50 again, the breakout has failed.
steps.tip: Two peaks aren’t a double top until the trough breaks.

steps.title: Triangles
steps.body:
• **Symmetrical:** lower highs and higher lows that converge. It can break either way.
• **Ascending:** flat ceiling and higher lows. It usually breaks upwards.
• **Descending:** flat floor and lower highs. It usually breaks downwards.

Volume tends to fall while it forms and to rise on the breakout.

steps.title: Flags and rectangles
steps.body:
• **Flag:** after a strong, fast move (the **flagpole**), a few days in a small rectangle tilted against the trend. It lasts **less than 3 weeks**. If it’s a small triangle, it’s a **pennant**.
• **Rectangle:** a sideways range between clear support and resistance; a breakout on volume usually sets the direction.

steps.title: The data on flags (Bulkowski)
steps.body: In a bull market, they break upwards **60 %** of the time; the average move after the breakout is around **9 %**, and they **fail** (don’t even advance 5 %) in roughly **44–45 %** of cases.
steps.key: Continuation patterns are the market catching its breath, although sometimes it turns.
steps.tip: A flag is a pause for breath, but almost half the time the runner runs out of air.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body:
A **false breakout** happens when the price gets past a level for a few days… and then falls back inside. Whoever bought the breakout is trapped.

It happens a lot: according to Bulkowski, the H&S fails 19 % of the time and flags around 44 %.

steps.title: How to filter them
steps.body:
• Wait for a **close** on the other side, not just a wick.
• Look for above-average **volume** on the breakout.
• Some traders require the close to clear the level by **1–3 %**.
• Check whether the broken level holds on the return (role reversal).

steps.title: And if it fails, the stop
steps.body: No filter gets rid of them all. That’s why the stop goes where the breakout stops making sense: back inside the zone, below the last relevant low. And the position size is set so that this failure costs little.
steps.key: A breakout without a close or volume is just an excursion.
steps.tip: Before you enter a breakout, decide where you’ll admit it was false.

u21l1-1.prompt: In this sideways stretch, tap the ceiling: the highest close, where sellers showed up (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · August–October 2024)
u21l1-1.explanation: That zone acts as resistance: the rise stalled there and the price fell back.

u21l1-2.prompt: Now the floor: tap the lowest close, where buyers showed up (NVIDIA · closes every 3 sessions · December 2025 – February 2026)
u21l1-2.explanation: That zone acted as support: the fall stalled and the price bounced strongly.

u21l1-3.prompt: You’ve bought at the last price. Place the stop a little below the support: the recent low.
u21l1-3.explanation: If the price loses the support, the buy idea is no longer valid. The stop goes a little below, not right on the line, so that a wick doesn’t trigger it.

u21l1-4.prompt: Now place the target: near the resistance, the previous high.
u21l1-4.explanation: Selling tends to show up at the previous high: putting the target in that zone is more realistic than waiting for it to break through.

u21l1-5.prompt: Support levels should be drawn as lines exact to the cent.
u21l1-5.explanation: They’re zones where lots of people agree, not an exact price.

u21l1-6.prompt: What makes a support level more relevant? Select all that apply.
options: That an ad on social media says so
That there was a lot of volume in that zone
That the price has turned there several times
u21l1-6.explanation: More touches, more volume and more recent. Old, distant levels carry less weight.

u21l1-7.prompt: Look for support and resistance in these 30 candles. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l1-7.explanation: Support or resistance tells you where buying or selling may appear, not what will happen. Above all, it shows you where you’ve been proved wrong.

u21l1-8.prompt: Pablo bought at €50, the share fell to €40 and now it’s back at €50. Lots of people like him want to «get their money back». What usually happens in that zone?
options: Selling tends to appear: it acts as resistance
The price is sure to shoot up
Nothing special: €50 is a price like any other
u21l1-8.explanation: Resistance comes from traders’ memory: those who lost want to get out without a loss.
feedback: Exactly: the memory of those who bought higher creates supply at that level.
It might break through, but it usually struggles: there are sellers waiting there.
It’s exactly where lots of trapped buyers want out: selling tends to appear.

u21l1-9.prompt: Quick: a zone where falls have stalled several times.
u21l1-9.explanation: It’s support: that’s where buyers showed up.

u21l1-10.prompt: There’s support around €20. You put the stop 3 % below. At what price does it go?
u21l1-10.explanation: 20 × 0.97 = €19.40. Leaving a bit of margin stops a mere wick from knocking you out.

u21l2-1.prompt: The price breaks strongly through resistance at €50 and, weeks later, comes back to €50. What role does that level usually play now?
u21l2-1.explanation: It’s the role reversal: the old ceiling tends to act as a floor.

u21l2-2.prompt: Support at €30 held for a year. Today the price closes at €27 on heavy volume. Days later it bounces back to €30. Laura owns shares and hopes it will «go up again like before». What’s most likely at €30?
options: That the level no longer matters
That it meets selling: the old support may act as resistance
u21l2-2.explanation: Support broken on volume often turns into resistance.
feedback: Broken levels tend to matter even more: lots of people remember them.
It could happen, but now there are sellers there: those who bought at the support want out without a loss.
That’s the role reversal. It’s not certain, but it’s what you should watch.

u21l2-3.prompt: Bruno bought after resistance at €100 was broken. The price rises to €106 and falls back to €101. What’s the sensible thing to do?
options: Buy three times as much to average down
Sell in a panic: it’s all over
Watch whether €100 holds as support; his stop was already below that zone
u21l2-3.explanation: Returning to the broken level is normal; what matters is whether it holds.
feedback: Adding more without a plan in the middle of the uncertainty multiplies the risk.
Retesting the broken level is very common. If it holds above €100, the breakout is still alive.
Good: if the old ceiling holds as a floor, the idea is still valid; if it closes clearly back inside, the breakout was false.

u21l2-4.prompt: You’ve bought at the last price. Place the stop where the idea stops being valid: below the last relevant low.
u21l2-4.explanation: Below the recent low, the structure that justified buying breaks down.

u21l2-5.prompt: Place the target at the previous high, where selling appeared before.
u21l2-5.explanation: The previous high is resistance: it’s reasonable to expect selling there and take profits.

u21l2-6.prompt: No name, no date. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l2-6.explanation: A level switching roles is common, not guaranteed. That’s why every idea comes with a stop on the other side of the level.

u21l2-7.prompt: Another real chart. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l2-7.explanation: Levels help you decide where to get in and where to get out if you’re wrong; they don’t predict the outcome.

u21l2-8.prompt: After a breakout, what role does the level usually play?
u21l2-8.explanation: What breaks upwards tends to start holding the price up; what breaks downwards, to hold it back.

u21l2-9.prompt: After breaking a level, the price often comes back to test it before moving on.
u21l2-9.explanation: It’s very common: in the H&S, for example, it returns to the neckline 68 % of the time.

u21l2-10.prompt: When the price breaks out upwards and then returns to the broken level, Bulkowski calls it a ____.
u21l2-10.explanation: After a downside breakout, the return is called a pullback.

u21l3-1.explanation: Two higher lows draw it and a third touch confirms it.

u21l3-2.prompt: Look at the lows: what trend do they show? (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · July–September 2025)
u21l3-2.explanation: Each low is above the previous one: you could draw an uptrend line underneath.

u21l3-3.prompt: Now look at the highs: what trend do they show? (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2025)
u21l3-3.explanation: The highs keep getting lower: a downtrend line would connect them from above.

u21l3-4.prompt: To draw the downtrend line you need the starting point: tap the highest close (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · December 2025 – February 2026)
u21l3-4.explanation: It’s the first close: from there, each high was lower. The downtrend line would connect that peak with the following highs.

u21l3-5.prompt: In this rise, tap the lowest close: the start of the uptrend line (NVIDIA · closes every 3 sessions · March–May 2026)
u21l3-5.explanation: From that low, each dip stopped higher: it’s the line’s first anchor point.

u21l3-6.prompt: Breaking an uptrend line always means a downtrend is starting.
u21l3-6.explanation: A sideways phase may begin. You need to look at it together with the structure of highs and lows.

u21l3-7.prompt: Which scale is best for drawing trendlines over several years?
u21l3-7.explanation: On a linear scale, an exponential trend seems to break its line when it doesn’t.

u21l3-8.prompt: If you draw a parallel line through the highs of an uptrend, you get a ____.
u21l3-8.explanation: Inside the channel, the lower edge acts as support and the upper edge as resistance.

u21l3-9.prompt: Quick: what’s the minimum number of higher lows you need to draw an uptrend line?
u21l3-9.explanation: Two draw it; a third touch confirms it.

u21l3-10.prompt: Ana draws an almost vertical trendline after a 40 % rise in three weeks. What do you tell her?
options: To delete the line and buy more
That it will probably break soon, and that breaking it won’t mean it’s the end of everything
u21l3-10.explanation: Slopes of 30–45 degrees are more sustainable; vertical ones end in sharp corrections.
feedback: Ignoring the risk of such a steep rise isn’t a plan.
Exactly: such a steep line breaks easily, and the break may just lead to a sideways phase.
Very steep lines tend to break soon: a rise like that is hard to sustain.

u21l4-1.prompt: Put the formation of a head and shoulders in order.
options: Right shoulder, lower than the head
u21l4-1.explanation: The pattern only exists once the last step arrives: the neckline break.

u21l4-2.prompt: When is a head and shoulders confirmed?
options: When the price closes below the neckline
u21l4-2.explanation: Before the breakout, it’s only a possibility.

u21l4-3.prompt: Head at €120 and neckline at €100. What’s the classic target after the breakout?

u21l4-4.prompt: Head at €120 and neckline at €100. What’s Bulkowski’s cautious target, using half the height?
u21l4-4.explanation: Half the height: €10. 100 − 10 = €90. Only 51 % reach the full target.

u21l4-5.prompt: Inverse H&S: head (the low) at €40 and neckline at €50. Classic target after breaking upwards?
u21l4-5.explanation: A height of €10, projected upwards from €50: €60.

u21l4-6.prompt: Before looking for shoulders, find the summit: tap the highest close in this stretch (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · September–November 2024)
u21l4-6.explanation: In an H&S, the head would be that peak. But to call it a pattern you’d need two lower shoulders and, above all, a neckline break.

u21l4-7.prompt: According to Bulkowski, almost every H&S reaches its classic target.
u21l4-7.explanation: Only 51 %. That’s why he suggests a target of half the height.

u21l4-8.prompt: Nasdaq 100, March 2000, after years of strong gains. What do you think happened next?
u21l4-8.explanation: Reversal patterns are confirmed when their key line breaks, and you only see that afterwards. At the top, nobody has that confirmation yet.

u21l4-9.prompt: Quick: which line connects the lows between the head and the shoulders?
u21l4-9.explanation: The neckline: when it breaks, the pattern is confirmed.

u21l4-10.prompt: A share has formed two shoulders and a head, but hasn’t broken the neckline yet. Pablo wants to sell everything now «to get ahead of it». What do you tell him?
options: To buy more: the pattern is bullish
Good: getting ahead always pays off
That the pattern isn’t confirmed until there’s a close below the neckline
u21l4-10.explanation: No breakout, no pattern. Getting ahead of it means betting on something that doesn’t exist yet.
feedback: The (non-inverse) H&S is a bearish pattern: that idea makes no sense.
Without a breakout, the pattern doesn’t exist: many end in new highs.
Exactly: until the breakout it’s only a possibility. And even when confirmed, it fails 19 % of the time.

u21l5-1.explanation: Two similar peaks with a trough in the middle.

u21l5-2.prompt: Quick: when is a double bottom confirmed?
options: When the price clears the high in between
When it makes the second low
u21l5-2.explanation: Until then, it’s just two lows.

u21l5-3.prompt: Double bottom: lows at €40 and a high in between at €50. Classic target after clearing €50?

u21l5-4.prompt: Double top: peaks at €80 and trough at €72. Classic target after losing €72?

u21l5-5.prompt: Ana sees an «almost formed» double top and sells before the price breaks the low in between. What mistake is she making?
u21l5-5.explanation: Patterns are confirmed when their key line breaks, not by their shape.
feedback: She’s getting ahead of a pattern that doesn’t exist yet: many turn out to be pauses before new highs.
Quite the opposite: she’s selling before she has the confirmation.
Exactly: without a break of the trough there’s no double top, just two peaks.

options: Two similar peaks and the price still above the trough
Two similar lows and a close above the high in between
Two similar lows and a wick touching the high in between
Two similar peaks and a close below the trough
u21l5-6.explanation: You need a close on the other side of the key line. A wick isn’t enough.

u21l5-7.prompt: Tap the lowest close in this stretch: in a double bottom, it would be one of the two lows (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2025)
u21l5-7.explanation: Buyers showed up there and the price bounced. To call it a double bottom you’d need a second similar low and a break above the high in between.

u21l5-8.prompt: Look at the latest highs and lows. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l5-8.explanation: A half-formed pattern is only a hypothesis. Until it breaks its key line, it could go either way.

u21l5-9.prompt: Another real chart, no name. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l5-9.explanation: Looking for Ms and Ws on every chart is tempting; the eye finds shapes everywhere. That’s why a breakout is required.

u21l5-10.prompt: A double top is confirmed as soon as the price makes the second peak.
u21l5-10.explanation: It’s confirmed when the low of the trough between the two peaks breaks.

u21l6-1.prompt: Match each pattern with its shape.
u21l6-1.explanation: The shape tells you who’s pushing: in the ascending one, the buyers; in the descending one, the sellers.

u21l6-2.prompt: Match each part with its definition.
u21l6-2.explanation: Flagpole, pause and breakout: that’s the story of a continuation pattern.
right: Small rectangle tilted against the trend
Exit from the pattern, ideally on volume

u21l6-3.prompt: Which way does it usually break?
u21l6-3.explanation: Ascending and descending triangles have a bias; symmetrical triangles and rectangles depend on the breakout.

u21l6-4.prompt: A rectangle is a sideways range. What trend does this stretch have? (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · August–October 2024)
u21l6-4.explanation: The price swings between a ceiling and a floor and ends up almost where it started: that’s what a rectangle looks like.

u21l6-5.prompt: According to Bulkowski, what percentage of flags fail (don’t even advance 5 %) in bull markets?
u21l6-5.explanation: They’re short-range patterns: almost half don’t even reach 5 %.

u21l6-6.prompt: Volume usually falls while a triangle is forming.
u21l6-6.explanation: And it usually rises on the breakout.

u21l6-7.prompt: Can you see a pause after a strong move? Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l6-7.explanation: Even if it were a textbook pattern, a flag fails almost half the time according to Bulkowski. The pause doesn’t tell you how it ends.

u21l6-8.prompt: Another chart, no name, no date. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l6-8.explanation: Continuation patterns offer modest probabilities. The real decision is how much you risk if they fail.

u21l6-9.prompt: Quick: a «flag» that lasts two months…
options: Is more of a rectangle or a channel

u21l6-10.prompt: A flag normally lasts less than ____ weeks.
u21l6-10.explanation: If it lasts longer, it’s called a rectangle or a channel.

u21l7-1.prompt: What reduces the risk of getting caught in a false breakout? Select all that apply.
options: Requiring the close to clear the level by 1–3 %
Jumping in on the first wick that pokes through
Waiting for a close on the other side
u21l7-1.explanation: The first wick is exactly what traps most people in false breakouts.

u21l7-2.prompt: Resistance at €100. Today the price reaches €101.50 during the session but closes at €99.20 on low volume. Marta bought at €101 when she saw «the breakout». What happened?
options: She bought an excursion that wasn’t confirmed
She got into a confirmed breakout
She did the right thing: you have to get in before anyone else
u21l7-2.explanation: A breakout is confirmed by the close and the volume, not by the wick.
feedback: Exactly: without a close above and without volume, there’s no breakout. If she had no stop, she’s now trapped.
No: it closed below the level on low volume. It was a wick, not a breakout.
Getting in before confirmation is the classic way to fall for a false breakout.

u21l7-3.prompt: There’s resistance at €50. You require the close to clear it by 2 % before you treat it as broken. Above what price must it close?

u21l7-4.prompt: You’ve bought after a breakout. Place the stop where the breakout would stop making sense: below the last relevant low.
u21l7-4.explanation: If the price drops back below the recent low, the breakout has failed and the idea is no longer valid.

u21l7-5.prompt: Another case: place the stop below the recent low.
u21l7-5.explanation: Just below the recent low, with a bit of margin: that’s where you admit the mistake.

u21l7-6.prompt: You have €10,000 and, if the breakout turns out to be false, you want to lose 1 % at most. Choose the stop and the amount.
u21l7-6.explanation: First the stop (where the breakout fails), then the amount: with a maximum risk of €100, the further away the stop, the fewer shares you can buy.

u21l7-7.prompt: Another real chart, no name, no date. Up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u21l7-7.explanation: Not even breakouts on volume guarantee anything. What you can control is where you get out if they fail and how much you lose.

u21l7-8.prompt: If the price gets above resistance with just a wick and closes below it, the breakout is confirmed.
u21l7-8.explanation: A wick confirms nothing: you need a close on the other side, ideally on volume.

u21l7-9.prompt: Quick: what best confirms a breakout?
options: A wick on the other side
A close on the other side on high volume
u21l7-9.explanation: Close plus volume: lots of people behind the move.

options: If it closes clearly back inside and hits your stop, the idea has failed: you get out and learn
Buy more to lower your average price
Yes, hold on as long as it takes
u21l7-10.explanation: False breakouts are part of the game: the stop decides how much they cost.
feedback: That’s it! That’s what the stop is for. A false breakout with a stop is a small cost; without one, it can be huge.
Averaging down on an idea that has already failed usually makes the loss bigger.
If the breakout has failed, holding on without a plan turns a small mistake into a big one.
